title: Count Number of Teams
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every triple directly versus fixing the middle index and counting smaller/larger values on each side.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array rating of soldiers' ratings, return the number of ways to form a team of exactly 3 soldiers, at indices i, j, k with i less than j less than k, such that either rating[i] is less than rating[j] is less than rating[k], or rating[i] is greater than rating[j] is greater than rating[k] (strictly increasing or strictly decreasing).

blocks.text: Count every valid team of 3 soldiers (by index order) whose ratings are either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing from left to right.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Valid 3-Person Height Lineups
blocks.text: Picture lining up people by position, and counting every trio (in position order) whose heights are either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing left to right, like a mini "ascending or descending staircase" of three people.

blocks.caption: Fix the middle soldier; count smaller/larger ratings on each side to combine into valid teams

blocks.text: There are 3 valid teams: for example, (2,3,4) is increasing, and (5,4,1), (5,3,1) are decreasing.
Before checking every triple directly, notice that fixing the MIDDLE index and counting smaller/larger values on each side directly gives the number of valid teams centered at that middle index.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For a fixed middle index j, an increasing team needs i to its left with a smaller rating, and k to its right with a larger rating.

Observation 2: A decreasing team similarly needs i to its left with a larger rating, and k to its right with a smaller rating.

Observation 3: Counting how many ratings to the left of j are smaller (or larger) than rating[j], and similarly to the right, gives everything needed: multiply "smaller to the left" by "larger to the right" for increasing teams, and "larger to the left" by "smaller to the right" for decreasing teams.

Observation 4: Summing these products over every possible middle index j gives the total count of valid teams.
This leads to fixing each index as the middle of a potential team, counting smaller and larger ratings on each side directly, and combining those counts into the two team types.
Check every index triple i less than j less than k directly for the strictly increasing or strictly decreasing condition.

items: Loop over every triple of indices i less than j less than k.
Check whether rating[i], rating[j], rating[k] is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every triple of indices is generated and checked directly against the increasing or decreasing condition.
No structure or counting is reused between triples that share the same middle index j.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed), every triple examined directly.
Space: O(1) extra.
Limitation: for a fixed middle index j, every valid (i, k) combination can be counted directly from the counts of smaller/larger values on each side, without checking each pair individually.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every (i, k) pair for a fixed j is unnecessary: only the COUNTS of smaller and larger ratings on each side of j matter, not which specific indices they are.

What to count for each j: how many ratings to the left of j are smaller than rating[j], how many are larger, and the same for the right side.

How to combine these counts: increasing teams centered at j need (smaller to the left) times (larger to the right); decreasing teams need (larger to the left) times (smaller to the right).

The core idea: for each j, count smaller/larger ratings on both sides directly, and add both product terms to the running total.

For every index j, count how many earlier indices have a smaller rating, how many have a larger rating, and do the same for later indices. Add (smaller-left times larger-right) plus (larger-left times smaller-right) to the running total.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: for each middle index, count smaller/larger on each side, combine directly

blocks.text: Every valid team is uniquely determined by its middle index j, together with a choice of one smaller-left-index (or larger-left-index) and one matching larger-right-index (or smaller-right-index). Multiplying the counts on each side directly enumerates every such combination without needing to check individual (i, k) pairs, since any smaller-left index paired with any larger-right index forms a valid increasing team, and similarly for decreasing.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), for each of n middle indices, one O(n) scan of both sides.
Space: O(1) extra.

blocks.text: Count Number of Teams shows how fixing the MIDDLE element of a 3-element pattern, and counting matching values on each side directly, replaces checking every (left, right) pair with a single multiplication.

items: Forgetting the decreasing case, only counting strictly increasing teams.
Double-counting by not cleanly separating "smaller" and "larger" counts on each side (values are guaranteed distinct here, simplifying this).

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every triple", think: fix the middle index, count smaller/larger values on each side, and multiply.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n cubed) time; the optimized fix-the-middle approach runs in O(n squared) time. Both use O(1) space.

items: Pattern: fix the middle index of a 3-element pattern, count matching values on each side, and multiply.
Core Idea: for each middle index, count smaller/larger ratings to its left and right; combine (smaller-left times larger-right) plus (larger-left times smaller-right) into the running total.
Time: O(n cubed) for the brute force, O(n squared) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: fixing the middle index turns pairwise checking into direct multiplication of side counts.
Interview Difficulty: a clean example of exploiting the "middle pivot" structure in a 3-element pattern.
One line memory trick: fix the middle, count smaller/larger on each side, multiply and sum.
